newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin signs Duma bill on chemical arms disposal.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin signs Duma bill on chemical arms disposal.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin signed into law on Friday a bill approved last week by the communist opposition-dominated Russian parliament that sets out how Moscow will get rid of its chemical weapons, but not when.

The Kremlin press service said in a statement: "The law establishes the legal basis for the implementation of a range of work for destroying chemical weapons stored on Russian territory and for ensuring the safety of citizens and protecting the environment while the necessary work is carried out."

The State Duma lower house resisted pressure from the Kremlin and abroad to ratify a treaty banning chemical weapons, saying it needed more time and Western cash to destroy its deadly stockpile. The pact came into force on Tuesday.
Yeltsin's spokesman said on Tuesday the Duma's actions had put Russia in a "delicate position" since without ratifying the treaty it cannot participate in further deliberations.
The Duma asked other countries last week for special consideration for Russia's money problems and urged that Moscow still be given a say in forthcoming negotiations.
The deputies said they aimed to ratify the treaty in a few months and backed the draft law that lays down how, but not when, Russia will destroy its weapons.
"The State Duma...has begun the process of ratifying the convention and intends to complete it if possible this autumn if the necessary conditions are met," said the statement.

The 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention, which took years to negotiate, bans the production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons. The treaty obliges members to eliminate all chemical weapons and production facilities by 2007.
Officials estimate it could cost $5 billion or more for Russia to destroy its 40,000 tonnes of chemical weapons, many of which are kept in ageing and unsafe facilities.
